extracted.intended_audience: scientists and researchers (readers and contributors to Nature); practitioners and authors of scientific books, manuals, and letters
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and implicit standards for reviewing scientific books, manuals, and letters to a research journal, plus the journal's submission/acceptance policy. Covers criteria for clarity, accuracy, methods reporting, nomenclature, experimental demonstration, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal submission policy (Letters/Manuscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for unsigned letters; he cannot be expected to return, or to correspond with the writers of rejected manuscripts intended for this or any other part of Nature. No notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for contributors: do not send anonymous communications; expect no correspondence or return of rejected manuscripts; letters should be signed. This is a procedural requirement rather than evaluative scoring guidance, but affects how submissions are handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and explicitness of methods in a practical methods book
rubrics_metrics.description: A methods book should teach practitioners to carry out a proper investigation of gastric contents (or analogous procedures) instead of simply guessing at causation; it must give sufficiently explicit details for those working out the methods themselves (e.g., indicate what the colour-changes consist of when an indicator is used and make the rationale of particular methods sufficiently clear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive indicators: explicit step-by-step descriptions, explanations of reagent/indicator behaviour, rationale for procedures (e.g., Topfer's method), and enough detail to reproduce methods. Anti-patterns: omitting descriptions of observable diagnostic changes or the reasons a test works; being 'hardly explicit enough' for practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of methods based on practical value and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may confine themselves to chemical methods and be 'eclectic in treatment, mentioning only the methods which they have found during twelve years' trial of practical value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: prefer inclusion of methods tested in practice over exhaustive theoretical lists. Guidance: indicate practical trial period or experience backing the methods; highlight methods shown useful in real practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and seasonal correctness of natural-history illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should accurately represent the subject (e.g., seasonal colouration and ear-tuft presence in squirrels). Plates that depict a winter appearance in a summer scene are misleading and condemn the work for the naturalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify illustrations against natural history facts and seasonal variation. Anti-pattern: showing species in impossible combinations of seasonal traits (e.g., ear-tufts and chestnut winter tail in summer foliage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate tone and audience suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A book should suit its intended readers: a sound book on natural history or a good novel — attempts to combine the two may not appeal; text should commend itself to the target audience (e.g., juvenile readers vs. specialists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether style, tone, and structure match the intended readership. Anti-patterns: mixing novelistic storytelling with scientific description in ways that reduce credibility or appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a useful scientific manual (e.g., limnology)
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful manual should summarise the methods of observation which experience has shown to be the best, include descriptions of the instruments used, the improvements recently introduced in them, and the principal results hitherto obtained; appendices with lists/data (e.g., positions and areas of principal lakes) are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist for manuals: (1) practical observation methods, (2) instrument descriptions and recent improvements, (3) summary of principal empirical results, (4) useful appendices/data tables, (5) adequate bibliographic references to foundational works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of valuable mathematical research publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical works should show a serious purpose to adhere only to real problems, with great analytical facility, clearness and fastidious elegance, and immeasurable patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical writing for problem relevance, analytical power, clarity of exposition, elegant presentation, and thoroughness. Anti-patterns: lack of teaching clarity is less important than adherence to substantial, genuine problems, but pedagogical defects may be noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report experimental/observational method details for atmospheric work
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting upper-air research (pilot balloons, kites), give apparatus and procedure: balloon nominal diameter, gas used (dry hydrogen made from zinc and sulphuric acid), method of observation (two observers on a kilometre baseline using theodolites), numbers/heights of ascents, and any mechanical apparatus for kites (winch design, power source).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting criteria: include number of trials, maximum heights reached, instrumentation specifications and manufacturers, observational geometry (baseline length / observer arrangement), and planned improvements. This allows reproducibility and assessment of data quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check theoretical statements against established principles and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific statements (e.g., about Newton's rings in polarised light) must accord with established theoretical results (Stokes, Fresnel, reversibility) and with experimental observation; errors in textbooks should be pointed out and corrected with reasoning and experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for claims: (1) show consistency with known physical principles, (2) cite authoritative sources, (3) perform or propose reproducible experiments to demonstrate the point. Provide both theoretical argument and experimental verification where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, reproducible demonstrations for pedagogical correction
rubrics_metrics.description: When correcting an error or illustrating a phenomenon, propose simple, easily performed experiments (e.g., oil film on a teacup viewed through a Nicol) that avoid objections of more elaborate demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical guidance: use accessible materials and clear observation protocols so readers can replicate experiments. Include expected observations and explanation of how these support the theoretical point.

rubrics_metrics.name: State assumptions and empirical basis for theoretical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Results that cannot be deduced from first principles (e.g., gain of entropy by slow diffusion at constant pressure and temperature) must be recognised as based on experimental evidence and may be treated as definitions or approximations (analogous to Boyle's law as part of the definition of a perfect gas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting theory, explicitly state what follows from laws/definitions and what must be assumed from experiment; clarify applicability and limitations to 'actual' vs 'perfect' models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for scientific nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: A name should connote some of the distinctive properties of the thing named; adopt systematic nomenclature (e.g., Rutherford's scheme: parent element name plus letters X, A, B, C...), and avoid fanciful meaningless names for radioactive products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming guidance: prefer established, systematic conventions that indicate relationships/properties; avoid hybrid or linguistically awkward coinages that do not aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe novel technical processes with materials, steps, advantages, and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: A new method (e.g., Warner-Powrie colour-photography) should be described in terms of what it does (triple-coloured lined screen with finer lines without gap/overlap), how it departs from previous methods (discarding ruling in favour of a printing method that removes registration difficulties), and the preparative steps and reagents (glass coated with bichromated colloid, exposure under black-lined screen, development, dyeing, fixing with formalin or chrome alum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For methodological innovations, include (1) clear statement of advantages, (2) complete procedural steps and materials, (3) comparison with earlier techniques, (4) notes on availability and expected timelines for adoption or limitations.
